newsitem.title: USA: Scholastic stock tumbles after loss forecast.
newsitem.headline: Scholastic stock tumbles after loss forecast.

text.p: Scholastic Corp.'s stock lost more than 40 percent of its value Friday, a day after the children's book publisher warned of a third-quarter loss and a decline in fiscal year earnings.
The sell-off was hastened as major Wall Street brokerages, including Merrill Lynch & Co., UBS Securities and Smith Barney, downgraded the stock and lowered Scholastic's earnings estimates.

The stock, which traded as high as $78.50 in the past year, sank as low as $33.25 on Nasdaq, where it was the biggest loser and one of the most active issues at midday. In two hours, Scholastic's trading volume reached almost 3 million shares, exceeding the average daily volume by 10 times. It was off $26 at $35.50 at midday.

After the market closed Thursday, Scholastic said it expects a loss of 70 cents to 80 cents per share in the third quarter ending Feb. 28. This includes 50 cents per share to cover a $13 million pretax charge related to reserves taken for retail book returns.
Scholastic also said it expects earnings of $1.45 to $1.60 per share for the fiscal year ending May 31, below the $1.97 posted last year.
The New York-based company earned $8.9 million, or 55 cents a share, on revenues of $216.1 million in the 1996 third quarter.
Scholastic said third-quarter results are weak because shipments of older titles in its leading "Goosebumps" children's book series declined, resulting in a drop in total shipments.

The third quarter is also affected by planned promotion costs for "Literacy Place," Scholastic's new core reading programme, even though it will have a modest benefit in the current fiscal year and a larger benefit in the next fiscal year, the company said.
Scholastic said it is committed to reducing costs where possible without adversely affecting future revenues.

UBS Securities analyst Edward Hatch said in a research note that Scholastic held a conference call with analysts soon after the announcement to "detail a dramatic and unforeseen shortfall in trade book sales at its major 'Goosebumps' franchise.
"In addition, an expected sales revival at its core book club business in the second half of fiscal ... 1997 has now been pushed out to fiscal 1998," Hatch said.
He suggested Scholastic appeared tardy in realising and reporting the sales trouble, calling into question "the veracity of its systems and response time in learning problems."

Two Wall Street firms recommended selling Scholastic's stock outright. Merrill Lynch slashed its near-term recommendation to "reduce" from accumulate, while Deutsche Morgan Grenfell declared the stock a "sell," down from "hold."

Deutsche Morgan analyst Rudolf Hokanson said that "'Goosebumps,' while still a very valuable brand, has slowed so dramatically its returns became 'frightening,' according to management" in the conference call.
Scholastic is a leading publisher and distributor of children's books, classroom and professional magazines, instructional materials and other educational products.
